replying_to: Replying to Graph2Tac: Learning hierarchical representations of math concepts in theorem proving
display_title: Official Review of Submission1459 by Reviewer WdSC

summary.value: This paper proposes a graph based approach for theorem proving with Coq. To do so, the authors propose to extract graph representations from existing Coq packages, and train a GNN that learns the meaning of definitions and other math symbols, namely G2T. The authors also enable G2T to incorporate unseen definitions by predicting their embeddings on the fly. The proposed method is evaluated on the separate Coq dataset, where it performs similarly to (sometime slightly better than) k-NN method.

strengths.value:
This work proposes to represent existing Coq proofs into graph and proposes a new GNN+RNN model to learn the graphs---This approach is interesting and seems novel to me, though I'm not familiar with the literature to be certain that no similar works were proposed before.

The overall methodology proposed in this work seems sound to me, though I'm not able to fully inspect the details due to lack of expertise in Coq and presentation issues (see weakness).

weaknesses.value:
Despite being a highly sophisticated model, Fig 5 suggests that G2T does not perform better than simple baselines such as k-NN:
- K-NN outperforms all pure G2T variants in terms of pass rate/sec for the most part, as the author pointed out, maybe for more complicated task G2T will have advantage, but it is not sufficiently demonstrated in the experiments.
- The only method outperforms k-NN is the hybrid one G2T+k-NN, which really cannot prove that G2T is a superior method as it is difficult to tell the contribution apart.
 
That said, I find the empirical significance of this work to be minor.
 
Other than that, the dataset created from the Coq package seems to be a good addition to the literature but there lacks too many details on how the dataset is created and processed, and further comparison to other datasets are needed for readers to assess its novelty and properly position it in the literature.

questions.value:
My main concern with the method is the online addition of definition embeddings. It is unclear to me how unknown definition is encoded and predicted without a text encoder. Judging from 3.1, definition nodes that are seen in the training set all get assigned with an embedding, then if an unseen definition comes, supposedly there is no embedding in the table that matches this definition, then how does one encode it into an embedding in the first place? Furthermore, it seems to me the definition task is essential for learning to represent unknown definitions, then for the G2T-NoDef model, how is unseen definition handled if there was not a definition task?

As a reader not familiar with Coq syntax, I find some technical parts very difficult to follow
 
It is Difficult to comprehend the diagrams in Fig 2, 3 and 4:
- For example, While the caption says Fig 2 is the graph representation of Fig 1, it is difficult to see the connections: what do "@" do "up_arrow" correspond to? What does different color mean in the graph? How is online update reflected in the graph representation? Why are there triangles with no symbols?
 
3.1 misses formal definitions of many important components making it difficult to track the architecture. For example:
- The RNN for local and global argument prediction
- The loss for definition and prediction task
- The formal representation of how new definitions are added to the current state, and how are they calculated into an embedding using the definition task.
- Fig 4 is not very helpful either---notations and names do not match very well with the text: what is "const embs"? are they trainable node labels? Which part corresponds to edge embeddings? Which parts correspond to "entry-point" nodes and "local context" nodes?

comment.value:
Thank you for your thoughtful review.

**On the empirical significance of our work**

As we mention in the common reply to all reviewers,
the k-NN solver was actually among state of the art in this field, better than existing works in this field.
We are the first paper to systematically compare it to other approaches and point this out.
We provide evidence that Graph2Tac outperforms any other neural or symbolic solvers available for Coq.

The k-NN is a strong approach with two advantages that many other solvers don't have.
Each call is fast, allowing it to explore an order of magnitude more states in a given time
(see Figure 9 in Appendix G _The Relative Speed of the Models_).
Also, it incorporates online proof information not seen during training
(see Figure 1).
Our G2T model not only rivals the state of the art k-NN despite being slower,
it is also a complementary approach to the online setting
of working in a package not seen during training.

Also, we see the main significance of our work is the introduction of a novel method that learns from the entire hierarchy of mathematical objects,
especially in an online setting. Our definition task improves G2T from 17.4% to 26.1% which is a 1.5x increase in theorems proved.

**On the definition task**

As for the definition task, we think there are some misunderstandings,
which we will try to make more clear in the paper:

> It is unclear to me how unknown definition is encoded and predicted without a text encoder.

For each new definition we have its definition body.
We uses graphs instead of text to encode new definitions, but otherwise it is similar to a text encoder.
The (graph of) the definition is put into our graph model, and the new definition embedding is the (pooled) output vector.
Graphs also let us build hierarchical representations, where the representation of a definition is
built from the embeddings of the component definitions.

When predicting a definition as an argument to a tactic, we select it from among all possible arguments in the global context.
This attention-like mechanism is step G in Figure 4.
(We will rename constant embeddings to definition embeddings in the Figure to be more clear.)

> Judging from 3.1, definition nodes that are seen in the training set all get assigned with an embedding,
> then if an unseen definition comes, supposedly there is no embedding in the table that matches this definition,
> then how does one encode it into an embedding in the first place?

Definitions seen during training use embeddings learned during training,
similar to how, say, a transformer model learns vocabulary embeddings.
Our definition task trains a graph model which can predict those learned embeddings.
If we encounter a new definition not seen during training, 
we use our definition graph model to predict its embedding.

> Furthermore, it seems to me the definition task is essential for learning to represent unknown definitions,
> then for the G2T-NoDef model, how is unseen definition handled if there was not a definition task?

The G2T-NoDef model uses learned embeddings for definitions seen during training.
At inference, any new embeddings get assigned random vectors (the `-Frozen` setting described in Section 3.1).

**Regarding clarifications of the figures**

We agree that Figure 2 could use more explanations. Unfortunately, the page limit prevents us from adding this. 
However, the graph dataset has been extensively
documented in a separate publication. An anonymized version can be found
[here](http://64.71.146.254:8000/SFyud_C5TmEq7AwnK9jaLsfTFMzgBl54cQ0pl2FJB-x9o2Hk24F4jO_W75RqGdOJ/papers/web-paper.pdf).
Regarding Figures 3 and 4, we agree they are complex.  We will attempt to clean them up and align them more with the text.
To answer your questions:
The edge and node embeddings are used in step A to initialize the embeddings of the graphs,
but we don't see how to put them in the figure.
We will relabel "constant embeddings" to be "definition embeddings" to match the text.
The entry point of the definition graph is the node labeled `f`.  Do you think we should label that?
It is unclear to us how to improve Figure 3.  Do you have suggestions on what could make the figures more clear?

**More technical details in 3.1**

We will clean up Section 3.1 and add more details (to that section or the appendix).

summary.value: This paper proposes Graph2Tac, a graph neural network-based approach to automating interactive theorem proving, particularly targeting the Coq proof assistant. Graph2Tac constructs a graph representing objects (e.g., local hypotheses) relevant to a proof goal in the Coq environment as well as global definitions. Four types of embeddings will be learned for edge labels, node labels, base tactics, and definitions in the training dataset, respectively.  The dataset is a set of Coq packages extracted from the Opam package manager, which consists of 520K definitions and 4.6 million proof state transformations. Graph2Tac communicates with the Coq theorem prover via _synth_ tactic and _Suggest_ command. The experimental evaluation shows that Graph2Tac achieves comparable performance with the classic k-NN-based machine learning approach and a combination of Graph2Tac and k-NN would outperform each individual approach.

strengths.value:
In general, the contributions of the current work are more about tooling and data collection rather than technical novelties of either theorem proving or machine learning. I can see the following strengths of this work:

- The graph construction systematically considers various information including proof states in the Coq kernel, global definitions, local variables, and equal terms (which are crucial in proofs by construction).
- The collected dataset represents the real-world applications for certified software
- Like kNN-based approaches, the tight integration with Coq's Tactician framework as well as solid engineering work make Graph2Tac practical to run on a consumer-grade computer. 
- Multiple baselines have been used in experimental evaluation on a wide selection of ITP tasks.

weaknesses.value:
The idea of using graph neural networks for automating interactive theorem proving is not new and the improvement is relatively minor, which is the main weakness of this work. More specifically,

- the general idea seems fairly incremental, however, on the other hand, the model architecture is quite complicated, which consists of GNN, several MLPs, argument RNNs, as well as bidirectional LSTM. It is difficult to see the effectiveness of different parts (e.g., are they all essential? Is GNN the most important component?)
- The title and abstract highlight learning hierarchical representations, however, there is no evidence supporting that hierarchy representations really make a big difference. 
- the improvement of Graph2Tac is not very significant, although combining Graph2Tac and k-NN by running them in parallel does give some interesting improvements, which is more like a simple engineering solution rather than a technical one.

questions.value:
Can you elaborate a bit more on the objective of the definition task? Shouldn't it be a (separate) pre-training task for learning good representations? 

Having an embedding for each definition might be too expensive. What is the size of the embedding table for definitions? 

Premise selection is one important step for theorem proving, which is not discussed in this work. How to guarantee that all relevant theorems/lemmas are properly included when constructing the graph representation?

comment.value:
Thank you for your review.  We plan to improve our writeup to address the important points you made.

**Response regarding incrementality and novelty**

We believe that our work provides strong novelty in that we are one of the first
that learns from the entire hierarchy of mathematical objects, especially in an
online setting. Our definition task improves G2T from 17.4% to 26.1% which is a
1.5x increase in theorems proved.

As we mention in the common reply to all reviewers,
the k-NN solver was actually among state of the art in this field, better than existing works in this field.
We are the first paper to systematically compare it to other approaches and point this out.

**Response regarding concerns regarding architectural complexity**

Much of the complexity is needed for tactic prediction.
Since we do not use a language model to generate tactics,
we need to predict both a base tactic, e.g. `rewrite _ in _`
and a sequence of arguments to go with that tactic,
which is why we need the RNN (or some other sequence model).
As for the bidirectional LSTM,
it is only used to embed definition names in the G2T-Named model.
We indeed show in our ablations that it does not improve results
(both in the experimental results
and in Appendix H _Ablation of G2T solvers and symmetry breaking with names_).

**Response regarding lack of evidence for effectiveness of hierarchical representations**

We didn't have an opportunity to explore in great detail the importance
of dependency depth in our hierarchical representations,
and we agree that would be interesting follow-up work.
Nonetheless, our ablations show that the hierarchical definition embedding task improves the G2T model from 17.4% to 26.1%,
highlighting the power of calculating new definitions embeddings from their definitions.
Further, in Figure 15, Appendix L _Impact of the Online Setting_,
we show that using the definition task doubles the pass rate if there are at least 10 new
dependencies in the global context.
This advantage increases as the number of unseen dependencies increases.
If your comment pertains to the fact that we are using learned embeddings for
definitions seen during training and computed hierarchical embeddings for definitions
not seen during training,
note that the learned definitions are trained to resemble the computed hierarchical embeddings
(and vice versa).
Additionally, we perform experiments
in Appendix H _Ablation of G2T solvers and symmetry breaking with names_
where for inference we recompute all embeddings to use the computed hierarchical embeddings.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Submission1459 by Reviewer UA5d

comment.value:
> Can you elaborate a bit more on the objective of the definition task?
> Shouldn't it be a (separate) pre-training task for learning good representations?

The definition task serves the purpose of aligning the learned definitions during training to the calculated definitions.
This way, during inference, if we encounter a new definition we can compute its embedding.
As for pretraining, would could have alternately learned our definition embedding computation as a pre-training task
via contrastive or non-contrastive self-supervised methods (like SimCLR, BYOL, VICReg, etc.).
However, by training them along with the final tactic prediction task it gives us a few advantages:
1. It lets us use learned embeddings when available and only swap to calculated embeddings for new definitions.
2. It ensures our calculated embedding is useful for the downstream task.
3. It prevents mode collapse where all embeddings become the same (since the embeddings have to be useful for the downstream task).
4. It allows us to share the weights of our GNN backbone on both the definition task and prediction task.
5. Since definitions are hierarchical (one definition depends on many previous ones),
   we need to store (or constantly recompute) embeddings of all intermediate definitions.
   (This is unique to our setting and not found in most other self-supervised learning papers.)
   The learned definition embedding table serves as a way to store and update intermediate embeddings.

> Having an embedding for each definition might be too expensive.
> What is the size of the embedding table for definitions?

Our table is indeed large, with about 459k entries (about an order of magnitude larger than the vocabulary table in small language model).
However, during argument selection we mask out all definition embeddings not in the current global context, significantly reducing the table size. Empirically, our approach is both fast and effective.
In Appendix H _Ablation of G2T solvers and symmetry breaking with names_,
we do show that if we used the G2T-Named model,
we could replace all the learned embeddings with calculated embeddings,
reducing the size of our model.
Other approaches in the literature based on premise selection also must compute embeddings for every theorem,
either beforehand or on-the-fly,
and the HOList models also learned embeddings for every definition.

> Premise selection is one important step for theorem proving, which is not discussed in this work.
> How to guarantee that all relevant theorems/lemmas are properly included when constructing the graph representation?

There might be a misunderstanding we will try to clarify.
We don't put background definitions in the graph passed to the model.
There are two types of graphs we deal with.
The large monograph contains the entire available mathematical universe, including all definitions (and theorems).
During training it contains all definitions in our training data.
During inference, it contains all definitions in Coq's current global context and is how data is communicated between Coq and the model.
This monograph is too large for our GNN models.
We instead break it up into its subgraphs (the different colors in Figure 2).
Our definition task uses only the subgraph for that particular definition cluster and no other.
The prediction task uses the subgraph for that proof state and no other definitions.

We don't need to do any preselection of premises.
Our models select arguments from all definitions (including lemmas) in the global context.
This argument selection is a form of premise selection predicated on the current proof state and the chosen base tactic.
It is accomplished via an attention-like mechanism in step G of Figure 4.
(Note: We will fix Figure 4 to say "definition embeddings" instead of "constant embeddings" to be more clear.)

summary.value: This paper proposes Graph2Tac, a novel neural-based theorem proving method that can better understand the new definitions defined in the test packages. Besides generating the next proof steps, Graph2Tac is also optimized to generate the embeddings of definitions so that for this definition the predicted embeddings are similar to the learned embeddings. This new training objective equip Graph2Tac the ability to embed the new definitions not seen during training. Graph2Tac is compared with baselines on a collection of Coq packages that are not presented during training. Compared to the Graph2Tac model trained for predicting the next steps only, the new definition prediction training could improve the performance on test set from 17.4% to 26.1%. Combined with a KNN baseline, Graph2Tac+KNN achieve the new start of the art results on the test benchmark.

strengths.value:
1 Define new concepts/theorems/methods is a fundamental feature of mathematics. This paper captures this key feature and works on an important and interesting online theorem proving settings where the theorem to prove contain unseen definitions presented in training. 
2 The proposed method is technically sound. By learning to predict the definition embeddings, the model could embed the novel definitions during inference. The design of GNN architecture is also reasonable.
3 Experiments demonstrate the benefits of training to generate definition embeddings.

weaknesses.value: Figure 4 is hard to follow for a new reader. It may help to remove some less important steps and intermediate results to make the figure more clear and helpful.

questions.value:
1 It is interesting to see if training to predict definition embeddings could be helpful to in general. Like for the test theorems without unseen definitions, or a Coq package that is largely covered by the training data, could the new training loss improve the results?
2 As mentioned in the paper, this new training objective utilize the hierarchical structure of definitions. It is interesting to see if the learning definition embeddings contain any implicit structures compared to training to generate the next steps only. For example, try to plot the definition embeddings using t-sne.

comment.value:
We would like to thank all the reviewers for their thorough
and detailed reviews, with many helpful comments.

We have revised the paper to address what we feel are the most important
criticisms. We are still working to amend the paper with other feedback. We will
inform the reviewers as we make revisions to the paper, and we will color code
major revisions to assist reviewing. Any revision in blue is responding to
multiple reviewers.

One common critique of our work is that our Graph2Tac solver with the definition
task only performs marginally better than the k-NN solver. The k-NN solver may
be perceived by many as a relatively weak solver due to its simplicity. It may
be surprising to many - including the authors of this paper - that the k-NN
solver is able to (significantly) outperform many others. 
However, the k-NN is a fast and powerful online solver which is able
to incorporate new information that other solvers cannot,
We believe we are the first work to systematically compare such a wide variety of approaches, and the
success of the k-NN model should be more widely known.

We'd also like to again stress that our main finding is that adding our novel
definition task to a graph-based solver significantly improves the results. The
approach of the k-NN is largely orthogonal to ours, and our results strongly
suggest that if one could also incorporate online information about new proofs
(as the k-NN does) into our G2T solver, it would lead to a solver that vastly
outperforms any other existing method. (Despite the strength of the k-NN solver,
opportunities for improvements are limited there. On the other hand, neural
solvers, like G2T, have much potential for future improvement.) That is our
reason for including the aggregate "G2T-Anon-Updated + k-NN" results.

To further highlight the strength of Graph2Tac and the k-NN versus other neural
solvers, we added Appendix B _Informal comparison on CoqGym test packages_
comparing our models against ASTactic, TacTok, and
ProverBot9001 on the CoqGym dataset. While the comparison is only informal, it
suggests the k-NN and our G2T solvers are state of the art for Coq in the
setting of testing on projects not seen during training.

Moreover, we also compare to a transformer baseline which has become the
defacto baseline of most recent works in this field.
The G2T and k-NN solvers, even the baseline G2T solver with no definition task,
all outperform the transformer.
This is even true in the setting where there are no new dependencies as shown in
Figure 15 in Appendix L _Impact of the Online Setting_.

comment.value: I share a similar concern. If the learned embedding really captures something interesting, it ought to outperform k-NNs, as the latter simply leverages surface syntax similarity. Another relevant concern I have is that the emphasis on "hierarchical" representation by authors is not backed up by evidence (i.e., no studies about hierarchical representations vs non-hierarchical representations). The so-called hierarchical representation in this work is essentially preprocessing with good premise selections by manually designed heuristics.

comment.value:
We will reply to concerns raised separately by reviewers in a single message.

> [Ursv] Also, I would expect to see that their approach has a clear edge over k-NN as number of never-seen definitions increases.
>
> [UA5d] If the learned embedding really captures something interesting, it ought to outperform k-NNs, as the latter simply leverages surface syntax similarity.

To verify the effectiveness of incorporating unseen definitions,
one should not compare to the k-NN solver, because both G2T and k-NN are online learners.
It is more appropriate to compare to offline learners, such as the transformer and G2T-NoDef-Frozen.

Both the k-NN solver and the G2T solver incorporate new information on-the-fly as shown in Figure 1.
However, the information employed by these models is highly orthogonal:

- The k-NN solver learns from new proof scripts and can exploit unseen
  user-defined tactics. On the other hand, while G2T learns from proof scripts
  in an offline setting, it cannot incorporate information from unseen proof
  scripts into its model on-the-fly. The k-NN does indeed only leverage surface
  syntax similarity, but in an online setting this is extremely powerful.
- The G2T solver can build an understanding of new math concepts, even when
  those concepts have never been seen during training. This understanding can
  then be exploited to gain a better understanding of the state of a proof and
  to predict novel arguments for tactics. On the other hand, the k-NN is
  completely oblivious to math concepts (it does not inspect the body of
  definitions at all) and is unable to predict novel tactic arguments (it sees
  tactics and their arguments as a black box).

Ideally, a model would employ both types of information,
and we "simulate" this by showing the performance of
G2T+k-NN. **Furthermore, because both models incorporate online information, there
is no reason to believe that the advantage of G2T over k-NN would increase as the
amount of unseen information increases.** On the other hand, looking at the pass-rate
per model call graph in the right half of Figure 5 does show
that G2T-Anon-Update has a strong per-model-call predictive advantage over the offline transformer and G2T-NoDef-Frozen solvers.
Additionally, Figure 15 in Appendix L shows that this advantage increases as the amount of unseen information increases.

> [UA5d] Another relevant concern I have is that the emphasis on "hierarchical" representation by authors is not backed up by evidence (i.e., no studies about hierarchical representations vs non-hierarchical representations).

We believe our hierarchical representation is natural given our objective.
Our objective was a proof state representation that takes new unseen definitions into account,
but without putting all previous definitions into the input (e.g. a long transformer prompt).
This requires representing the proof state as a structure, like a tree or a graph,
where each component definition has its own node which can be assigned a definition embedding.
It is then natural to use that same mechanism to compute those definition embeddings,
i.e. representing that definition also as a graph.
This leads naturally to a hierarchical representation where we first calculate the embedding for each
component and use that to calculate the embedding for later dependencies.

It is not obvious to us what a "non-hierarchical representation" would look
like in this setting.
There is no doubt that other effective approaches and improvements can
be devised. Nonetheless, we believe that the empirical effectiveness of our approach
stands on its own.

> [UA5d] The so-called hierarchical representation in this work is essentially preprocessing with good premise selections by manually designed heuristics.

We find this sentence particularly difficult to understand. We are familiar
with the concepts of "preprocessing through premise selection" and "manually designed
heuristics", and we see our work as quite distant from both of these concepts.
Could you explain in more detail what you mean?

> [Ursv] Do you think that the authors have done experiments to confirm effectiveness of handling never-seen definitions?
>
> [Ursv] I do see that there are some experiments related to "never-seen definitions" in the Appendix. But, considering that this should be the crucial advantage, it should definitely be in the main paper, and well explained.

A clear measure of the effective treatment for unseen definitions is the improvement of G2T-Anon-Update over G2T-NoDef-Frozen from 17.4% to 26.1%.
This is further reinforced by Figure 15 from Appendix L.

If there is a reviewer consensus that Figure 15 is more
valuable than Figure 7 in the main text, we can exchange them (including the
surrounding text) in the final revision. Otherwise, the page limit prevents us
from adding this information to the main text.

comment.value:
> [Ursv] I do believe that running the system in Figure 5 for more time would be useful. It might be the case that in the longer run your approach goes over the curve of k-NN, but it's unclear for how much.

Unfortunately, it is not computationally feasible to run the system for significantly
longer. We also believe that this would be of limited value. The G2T solver
already outperforms the k-NN solver by a marginal amount at the 10 minute mark.
This advantage may be extended slightly with a larger timeout. However, in any
case, the advantage will likely remain within the margin of error. As reviewer
ePHg rightly points out, our main contribution is not that we significantly
outperform the k-NN, but rather the introduction of a new online learning
technique for unseen definitions that is highly complementary to the online
techniques employed by the k-NN.

> [Ursv] Considering that the Venn diagram is important, can you make it more clear? (Current Figure is cut and even the caption can't be seen properly.)

Apologies. The layout of the paper was compromised after last week's update.
It has been restored.

> [Ursv] I do thus think that testing out combining other techniques with k-NN is crucial to testify about effectiveness of your work.

We believe that the Venn diagram in Figure 6 conclusively shows that the
combination of G2T and k-NN is the most powerful. To further back up this claim,
we have added a graph with additional combinations in Appendix O: _Additional
Combinations with the k-NN_ (Figure 20).

> [Ursv] Figure 5. It's still challenging to distinguish between different settings. Can you include distinct symbols for distinct lines; e.g.: triangles, circles, rectangles, etc.

We have updated Figure 5 to hopefully be more legible.

comment.value:
We're glad we could clarify things. Thanks for the interaction.

> I believe you should add these statements to the paper. Brief and clear description. Possibly in the related work.

We agree that a more focused comparison between the online techniques of the
k-NN and G2T would benefit the paper. The information is already present in the
current version, but perhaps not presented in the clearest way. We will work on
this for the final version (we are out of time to do it during the rebuttal
period).

> Additionally, If there are good references that support these claims, even better.

The online nature of the k-NN solver has been described in these publications.
Although they are cited in our work, we will try to make this more "prominent".

- [The Tactician: A Seamless, Interactive Tactic Learner and Prover for Coq](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-53518-6_17)
- [Online Machine Learning Techniques for Coq: A Comparison](https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-3-030-81097-9_5)

metareview.value: This paper leverages the Coq definition hierarchy in constructing tactics.  The main issue among the reviewers is that the performance does not dominate knn methods.  I am also concerned that the coq benchmark is not where most work in this area is focused and hence the competition may already be weaker than would be encountered on the LEAN mathlib benchmarks.
